entries.title: White Sox use patient approach, move to 4-1 on the year against AL strikeout leader Gavin Williams
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Add the White Sox’ performance in Game 2 of the American League Division Series to their four games in the regular season against Guardians starter <b>Gavin Williams</b> and it doesn’t look too bad at first for the AL strikeout leader.</p><p>Williams has a 3.91 ERA against the Sox, who have the AL’s best scoring offense. After punching out 11 in five-plus innings Monday in Cleveland, his strikeout rate against all hitters this year is a whopping 36.4%.</p><p>But he failed to earn the “W” in any of his starts against the Sox and has walked their hitters 10.3% of the time. The Guardians won just one of his five outings against the Sox, via a walk-off in extra innings in June.</p><p>“With the talented arms that the Guardians have, it is not just getting a good swing, you have to adjust,” said manager<b> Will Venable. </b>“You gotta find different ways to beat them.”</p><p>It gets worse: Williams failed to get through six innings in any of these outings, and an attempt to get him there Monday — facing the heart of the Sox’ order a third time — is where the game flipped in the visitors’ favor, giving the Sox a 4-3 win and a 2-0 edge in the best-of-five series.</p><p>Having already walked twice against Williams, <b>Miguel Vargas</b> worked a full count leading off the sixth inning before lining the seventh pitch he saw for a single. The hit chased Williams, who had entered the inning at 91 pitches, and kick-started the decisive three-run Sox rally against Guardians reliever <b>Erik Sabrowski</b>.</p><p>“[Williams] is a really good pitcher,” Vargas said. “My approach is focus on one pitch: middle-middle. I don’t think I’ve got much chance at anything else.”</p><p>Middle-middle is where the fastball Vargas singled on wound up being. He just had to make Williams work for a while.</p><p><b>Straight to the point for Taylor</b></p><p>After his four-inning outing in Game 1 on Saturday, it was up in the air whether reliever <b>Grant Taylor</b> would be physically able to pitch two days later. The answer came when he entered in the eighth inning Monday, weathering <b>Jo Adell</b>’s RBI triple to record a four-out save.</p><p>The conversation about his availability wound up being fairly short. Taylor said bench coach <b>Walker McKinven</b> approached him with a simple question: “You want it?”</p><p>“Obviously,” Taylor replied.</p><p><b>‘There’s hits in ice cream cones’</b></p><p>When <b>Sam Antonacci</b>, 23, told WGN on Sunday that he was eating an ice cream cone when Sox teammate <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> hit his two-run homer in Game  1, he noted he could have been in trouble with coaches if they’d needed him to pinch-hit and saw what he was doing.</p><p>But the Sox, with the youngest position-player group in the AL, see purpose in the snacks in the visitors’ clubhouse.</p><p>“I’ve noticed this in my baseball career: Ice cream cones are good luck,” said catcher<b> Kyle Teel</b>, 24. “There’s hits in ice cream cones.”</p><p>Venable has allowed his team to create their own clubhouse culture and stood by that approach in this case.</p><p>“I’m fully supportive of whatever these guys think is good luck,” Venable said. “Ice cream for everybody, then.”</p><p>Within reason at least. Antonacci–a lifelong infielder before this year–initially took a step in on Guardians outfielder <b>Steven Kwan</b>’s liner to left in the eighth, but held his focus to recover and make a scrambling catch for a crucial first out.</p><p>“Nice catch from Sam,” Vargas said. “I guess he wasn’t eating ice cream, so he made that play.”<br></p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: White Sox defy mistakes, expectations and physical limitations to take 2-0 lead in ALDS
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — In a pre-series scrum with White Sox beat writers last weekend, manager Will Venable warned that if the Sox yielded extra bases against the pesky American League Central-champion Guardians — be it through walks, errors or stolen bases — they’d lose.</p><p>By the time reliever Sean Newcomb’s throw to first skipped away in the first inning, allowing the Guardians to score two runs, the Sox had allowed the first two things to happen with only one out. It was yet another logical reason to expect them to come up short — or to fall back into the grim reality that defined most of their previous five years.</p><p>Instead, all the trouble melted away in a 4-3 victory in Game 2 of the ALDS.</p><p>When Brenton Doyle leaped at the wall to catch Patrick Bailey’s deep drive to center off Sox reliever Grant Taylor to end the game, the Sox were up 2-0 in the series, headed home for the first playoff game at Rate Field in five years and just one victory away from their first ALCS in 21 years.</p><p>“This is the identity of this team,” said infielder Miguel Vargas, who singled and scored in a decisive three-run sixth. “We know anybody here can have a huge at-bat and put us in the lead.”</p><p>Outfielder Braden Montgomery, a 2024 first-round draft pick by the Red Sox and a top-100 prospect, isn’t the most unlikely postseason hero after his two-out, two-run, go-ahead double off Guardians lefty Erik Sabrowski put the Sox up for good in the sixth. But Venable acknowledged before the game that Montgomery was a likely candidate to be replaced by a pinch-hitter against a left-hander after managing just a .430 OPS against lefties in the regular season.</p><p>Nevertheless, Montgomery prepared for Sabrowski like always and hit a first-pitch fastball down the right-field line in the sixth for one of the biggest Sox’ hits in years.</p><p>“He’s probably in the cage almost longer than anyone else,” Doyle said. “He really gives a crap about this game.”</p><p>It seemed questionable that Taylor would be available to pitch at all after logging four dominant innings to close out Game 1. As it turns out, he was slated to pitch one inning for a save if the situation came up, and he went one out longer than even that.</p><p>Three of his four outs were loud fly outs, wrapped around a booming triple by Joe Adell that reduced the Sox’ lead to a run. But style points aren’t what players concern themselves with in the playoff. Neither are whatever expectations this Sox team used to have.</p><p>A little over a year ago, Sean Burke was demoted to Triple-A Charlotte off a much weaker Sox roster. But on Monday, with midges swirling in the stadium in Cleveland, he picked up a game that threatened to spin out of control in the first and carried it until there were two outs in the eighth. He was pulled then after allowing his first hit in 5⅓ innings.</p><p>“I never thought the opponent would get a hit,” Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami boasted through his interpreter.</p><p>The Sox could have called an 84-win season a success without reaching the playoffs. Now they’re a win away from one of their deepest runs in franchise history. With a 36-45 road record this year, the Sox once looked like a team that needed their home environment to be successful. But four road playoff victories later, that has proven to be another misconception, another set of limitations to which the youngest group of position players in the league is not beholden.</p><p>For that, the young Sox have a hero’s welcome awaiting them in Chicago.</p><p>“I can’t place any expectations on it — I just know it’s going to be special,” Montgomery said of returning to their home field for Game 3 on Wednesday. “I can only imagine how the South Side is going to pop out in a couple of days. I can’t wait to see it and be a part of it.”</p>

entries.title: Police looking for man suspected of punching a woman on CTA platform
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are asking for help finding a man accused of punching a woman in the face on a South Loop CTA platform over the weekend.</p><p>The incident occurred at the Roosevelt CTA station about 11:55 a.m. on Sunday. The man is described as 35 to 40 years old, white or Hispanic and 5 feet 7 inches to 5 feet 10 inches tall. He was wearing a tan hooded sweatshirt, gray sweatpants and gray gym shoes without shoelaces. He has a thin mustache and short black hair, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information is asked to contact Mass Transit Detectives at 312-745-4447. Anonymous tips can be submitted at CPDTIP.com with the reference number RD JK-438007.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">AGGRAVATED BATTERY on <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/CTA?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#CTA</a> <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoCAPS01?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ChicagoCAPS01</a> (South Loop) <a href="https://x.com/Area3Detectives?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Area3Detectives</a> Mass Transit Detectives <a href="https://t.co/L8zuymcjqY">https://t.co/L8zuymcjqY</a> <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/ChicagoPolice?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#ChicagoPolice</a> <a href="https://t.co/HFLLXyObUY">pic.twitter.com/HFLLXyObUY</a></p>— Tom Ahern (@TAhern_) <a href="https://x.com/TAhern_/status/2107179509522759868?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: ‘She was a spark everywhere she went’ — Pilsen grieves one of its own
entries.summary: <p>Paola Judith Zamora Rojas' family gathered at her Pilsen apartment, as they have done many nights since her death.</p><p>Chairs faced an altar decorated with photographs of the 32-year-old mother. It was last Friday, the fourth evening of a nine-day Catholic novena.</p><p>Candles near the altar represented St. Jude. Zamora Rojas' older sister, Yahaira Gutierrez, said their mother, Sandra Zamora, prayed to the saint when Zamora Rojas stopped breathing during a near-death experience as a baby.</p><p>The family believes her survival was "some kind of miracle," Yahaira Gutierrez said. Sandra Zamora gave her daughter the middle name Judith in the saint's honor.</p><p>More than three decades later, St. Jude candles burned as the family prayed for her again.</p><p>Zamora Rojas had died by suicide Sept. 17 after what friends and relatives described as a long battle with mental illness.</p><p>Surrounding her family were traces of the life she had built: thrift-store records, vintage furniture and secondhand finds. Zamora Rojas' eye for fashion had earned her tens of thousands of followers on social media.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b00000" name="image-b00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c440c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0b71aea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0e478d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Paola Judith Zamora Rojas' mother, Sandra Zamora, places her daughter’s portrait on the wall during a prayer vigil for her daughter on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. Zamora Rojas died by suicide in September 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0e478d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3d01754/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0e478d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Paola Judith Zamora Rojas’ mother, Sandra Zamora, places her daughter’s portrait on the wall during a prayer vigil for her daughter on Friday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Octavio Jones/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Also attending was Diana Galicia Corona, whose son, Gabriel Cisneros, had been Zamora Rojas' fiancé .</p><p>Zamora Rojas was three months pregnant with their daughter, Olivia, when Cisneros, 22, died of an accidental heroin overdose on Mother's Day in 2016. She continued to call Galicia Corona her mother-in-law afterward. Galicia Corona said she called Zamora Rojas a "better-in-law."</p><p>A week before Cisneros died, Galicia Corona remembers leaving a Pilsen restaurant with the couple when music began playing, and her son took Zamora Rojas' hand, spun her around and danced with her on the sidewalk.</p><p>"What Gabriel and Paola had was a love story that should have never ended," Galicia Corona said.</p><p>Zamora Rojas never stopped grieving him, her family said. Galicia Corona saw that grief resurface around his birthday, holidays and the anniversary of his death.</p><p>Grief and depression were only parts of a life her family said was remarkably full.</p><p>Zamora Rojas was raising a daughter she adored, reselling clothing online, attending concerts and hosting traveling musicians in her home.</p><p>She showed new friends around Chicago and supported Pilsen artists and businesses, her family said.</p><p>And she often was the person others turned to when they were struggling.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Another said Zamora Rojas offered financial help despite her own money struggles.</p><p>"I want to make sure people know that Paola wasn't selfish," Yahaira Gutierrez said.</p><p>Yahaira Gutierrez said her sister worried about burdening others, sometimes keeping her pain to herself.</p><p></p><p>Zamora Rojas moved to Pilsen with her family when she was 2 or 3, Yahaira Gutierrez said. While their mother worked, the kids knew which neighbors they could call for help.</p><p>"Pilsen grew in her," Yahaira Gutierrez said. "And that's how she grew into Pilsen."</p><p>As an adult, shopping locally became part of her identity, friends and family said. </p><p>“A lot of her stuff is from somewhere else,” her brother, Cesar Gutierrez said, laughing about the phone calls he received from her asking for help moving furniture she found or thrifted. “You know how you usually go to Target and buy something brand new? She wouldn't go to Target.”</p><p>Zamora Rojas began thrifting as a child and later worked at Pilsen Vintage, where co-owners Paul Guizar and Maggie Reynoso said she was family.</p><p>She later sold her finds through <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/deadendvintagechicago?stkn=MWhjczY3dmplNHBwaQ==" target="_blank" >an Instagram account called Dead End Vintage</a>, modeling the clothing herself.</p><p>Galicia Corona said they dreamed of opening a Pilsen cafe that would double as a thrift store. entries.title: White Sox hold on for victory over Guardians to take 2-0 lead in ALDS showdown
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — In a pre-series scrum with White Sox beat writers last weekend, manager Will Venable warned that if the Sox yielded extra bases against the pesky American League Central-champion Guardians — be it through walks, errors or stolen bases — they’d lose.</p><p>By the time reliever Sean Newcomb’s throw to first skipped away in the first inning, allowing the Guardians to score two runs, the Sox had allowed the first two things to happen with only one out. It was yet another logical reason to expect them to come up short — or to fall back into the grim reality that defined most of their previous five years.</p><p>Instead, all the trouble melted away in a 4-3 victory in Game 2 of the ALDS.</p><p>When Brenton Doyle leaped at the wall to catch Patrick Bailey’s deep drive to center off Sox reliever Grant Taylor to end the game, the Sox were up 2-0 in the series, headed home for the first playoff game at Rate Field in five years and just one victory away from their first ALCS in 21 years.</p><p>“This is the identity of this team,” said infielder Miguel Vargas, who singled and scored in a decisive three-run sixth. “We know anybody here can have a huge at-bat and put us in the lead.”</p><p>Outfielder Braden Montgomery, a 2024 first-round draft pick by the Red Sox and a top-100 prospect, isn’t the most unlikely postseason hero after his two-out, two-run, go-ahead double off Guardians lefty Erik Sabrowski put the Sox up for good in the sixth. But Venable acknowledged before the game that Montgomery was a likely candidate to be replaced by a pinch-hitter against a left-hander after managing just a .430 OPS against lefties in the regular season.</p><p>Nevertheless, Montgomery prepared for Sabrowski like always and hit a first-pitch fastball down the right-field line in the sixth for one of the biggest Sox’ hits in years.</p><p>“He’s probably in the cage almost longer than anyone else,” Doyle said. “He really gives a crap about this game.”</p><p>It seemed questionable that Taylor would be available to pitch at all after logging four dominant innings to close out Game 1. As it turns out, he was slated to pitch one inning for a save if the situation came up, and he went one out longer than even that.</p><p>Three of his four outs were loud fly outs, wrapped around a booming triple by Joe Adell that reduced the Sox’ lead to a run. But style points aren’t what players concern themselves with in the playoff. Neither are whatever expectations this Sox team used to have.</p><p>A little over a year ago, Sean Burke was demoted to Triple-A Charlotte off a much weaker Sox roster. But on Monday, with midges swirling in the stadium in Cleveland, he picked up a game that threatened to spin out of control in the first and carried it until there were two outs in the eighth. He was pulled then after allowing his first hit in 5⅓ innings.</p><p>“I never thought the opponent would get a hit,” Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami boasted through his interpreter.</p><p>The Sox could have called an 84-win season a success without reaching the playoffs. Now they’re a win away from one of their deepest runs in franchise history. With a 36-45 road record this year, the Sox once looked like a team that needed their home environment to be successful. But four road playoff victories later, that has proven to be another misconception, another set of limitations to which the youngest group of position players in the league is not beholden.</p><p>For that, the young Sox have a hero’s welcome awaiting them in Chicago.</p><p>“I can’t place any expectations on it — I just know it’s going to be special,” Montgomery said of returning to their home field for Game 3 on Wednesday. “I can only imagine how the South Side is going to pop out in a couple of days. I can’t wait to see it and be a part of it.”<br></p>
